The active site is a conserved redox-active cysteine residue, the peroxidatic cysteine (C(P)), which makes the nucleophilic attack on the peroxide substrate. The peroxide oxidizes the C(P)-SH to cysteine sulfenic acid (C(P)-SOH), which then reacts with another cysteine residue, the resolving cysteine (C(R)), to form a disulfide bridge. The disulfide is subsequently reduced by an appropriate electron donor to complete the catalytic cycle. Although the primary sequence of this enzyme is similar to those of the 1-Cys Prx6 enzymes, its catalytic properties resemble those of the typical 2-Cys Prxs and C(R) is provided by the other dimeric subunit to form an intersubunit disulfide. Contains eight transmembrane regions plus two helical hairpins that dip into the membrane. These helical hairpin structures play an important role in the transport process. The first enters the membrane from the cytoplasmic side, the second one from the extracellular side. During the transport cycle, the regions involved in amino acid transport, and especially the helical hairpins, move vertically by about 15-18 Angstroms, alternating between exposure to the aqueous phase and reinsertion in the lipid bilayer. In contrast, regions involved in trimerization do not move

texts.value: Functions as an aminopeptidase (PubMed:15375159, PubMed:15713475, PubMed:15736957, PubMed:23696647, PubMed:41419167). It shows a preference for leucine as the N-terminal amino acid, but it can cleave several other amino acid residues (PubMed:15375159, PubMed:15736957). It is involved in protein degradation, probably performing degradation of oligopeptides produced by the proteasome into single amino acids (PubMed:15713475). In vitro, it can use various aminoacyl p-nitroanilide (aminoacyl-pNA) and aminoacyl 7-amino-4-methylcoumarin (aminoacyl-AMC) synthetic substrates, with a preference for leucine-pNA (PubMed:15375159, PubMed:15713475, PubMed:15736957, PubMed:23696647). It can also cleave moderately long polypeptide substrates of various compositions in a fairly unspecific manner (PubMed:15736957, PubMed:23696647). Lacks di- and tripeptidyl activity (PubMed:15736957). Has neither carboxypeptidase nor endoproteolytic activities, and is devoid of N-terminal deblocking activity (PubMed:15736957)
PhTET2 and PhTET3 can also interact physically and form stable heterooligomeric dodecameric complexes capable of breaking down very diverse polypeptidic chains with enhanced efficiency
Binds 2 divalent metal cations per subunit (PubMed:15375159, PubMed:15713475, PubMed:31217444). The in vivo cofactor is probably cobalt (PubMed:15736957).

The dimeric form of PhTET2 is active (PubMed:23696647). Oligomerization triggers the activity of PhTET2 toward large polypeptidic substrates (PubMed:23696647). The amidolytic activity is strongly stimulated by Co(2+) (PubMed:15736957). The presence of Zn(2+) and Mn(2+) causes around 50% inhibition at 0.5 mM, while slight or no effects are observed in the presence of Ca(2+) and Mg(2+) (PubMed:15736957). Inhibited by EDTA and bestatin in vitro (PubMed:15736957). Is insensitive to papain, antipain, chymostatin, leupeptin, pepstatin and aprotinin (PubMed:15736957)

kcat is 421.5 sec(-1) with Leu-pNA as substrate (for the dimeric form) (PubMed:23696647). kcat is 511 sec(-1) with Leu-pNA as substrate (for the dodecameric form) (PubMed:23696647). kcat is 31422 sec(-1) with Leu-pNA as substrate (PubMed:41419167). kcat is 1.5 sec(-1) with Met-Lys-bradykinin as substrate (for the dimeric form) (PubMed:23696647). kcat is 144.5 sec(-1) with Met-Lys-bradykinin as substrate (for the dodecameric form) (PubMed:23696647).
Optimum pH is 7.5 with Leu-pNA as substrate (PubMed:15736957). Strong activity is still detectable at pH 6 and 9 (PubMed:15736957).

Optimum temperature is 100 degrees Celsius over a broad pH array (PubMed:15736957). At temperatures lower than 70 degrees Celsius, less than 10% of the maximum activity is detected (PubMed:15736957). Is highly thermostable (PubMed:15736957). Shows half-lives of 24.8 minutes and 10.03 hours when incubated at 100 and 80 degrees Celsius, respectively (PubMed:15736957).

Homodimer (PubMed:23696647, PubMed:25171083). Homododecamer (PubMed:15375159, PubMed:15713475, PubMed:15736957, PubMed:16511005, PubMed:23696647, PubMed:25372688, PubMed:31217444). The assembly of six dimers results in a tetrahedral-shaped structure (PubMed:15375159, PubMed:15713475). All 12 active sites are located on the inside of the tetrahedron (PubMed:15375159, PubMed:15713475). Substrate access is granted by four pores with a maximal diameter of 18 Angstroms, allowing only small peptides and unfolded proteins access to the active site (PubMed:15713475). Beside the four entry pores, TET contains 12 small product release openings, which are large enough to allow passage of only single amino acid residues (PubMed:15713475). PhTET2 assembling is a non-random stepwise process in which hexamers represent the main intermediate (PubMed:23696647). In vivo, the dimeric precursor co-exists together with assembled TET complexes (PubMed:23696647). However, the homododecameric complex is extremely stable in solution and is not in dynamic equilibrium with free oligomeric forms of lower molecular mass (PubMed:25372688). The dimeric and dodecameric forms may perform different physiological roles (PubMed:23696647). The dodecamers are more efficient in hydrolyzing long polypeptide substrates as compared with the dimers (PubMed:23696647). PhTET2 can interact with PhTET3 and form heterododecameric complexes (PubMed:25171083, PubMed:25372688)

The enzyme cleaves polypeptides by a nonprocessive mechanism (PubMed:15736957). It does not process one substrate molecule completely before starting with another one (PubMed:15736957). Instead, the reaction products are generated by multiple rounds of substrate digestion (PubMed:15736957)
Belongs to the peptidase M42 family
